# Diverticulitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Diverticulitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/_H05Gh)

---

## Summary

Diverticulitis is a <u>diverticular disease</u> caused by inflammation of <u>colonic diverticula</u> and occurs as a complication of <u>diverticulosis</u>, more commonly in older adults. It may remain localized (mild <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>) or progress, resulting in complications such as <u>abscess</u> or perforation (<u>complicated diverticulitis</u>). Diverticulitis typically manifests with <u>fever</u> and <u>left lower quadrant</u> abdominal <u>pain</u> as the <u>sigmoid colon</u> is most commonly involved. CT abdomen with IV contrast is the preferred diagnostic modality in suspected acute diverticulitis. <u>Uncomplicated diverticulitis</u> usually responds to <u>conservative management</u> with bowel rest and <u>analgesics</u>; oral broad-spectrum <u>antibiotics</u> are reserved for patients at high risk of complications. In <u>complicated diverticulitis</u>, management consists of parenteral <u>antibiotics</u>, treatment of any complications, and, in some cases, emergency <u>colonic</u> resection. Once the acute phase has resolved, a <u>colonoscopy</u> is often performed to rule out <u>malignancy</u>. Elective <u>colectomy</u> is recommended for all patients with <u>complicated diverticulitis</u> that is <u>managed conservatively</u>. The procedure is not routinely indicated for <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>.




See also “<u>Diverticulosis</u>.”

---

## Definitions

Inflammation or infection of <u>colonic diverticula</u> (typically <u>false diverticula</u> caused by <u>weakness</u> in the intestinal wall)  [[2]](/library/amcQV10)[[3]](/library/rmcfS10)




![True diverticula and pseudodiverticula](media/w3eci4srrpy2d5ksxr907azu.jpg)

True diverticula and pseudodiverticula

![Types of diverticular disease](media/fmp9rifg1vqnheyylfv8qcyj.jpg)

Types of diverticular disease

## Pathophysiology

* Formation of <u>diverticula</u> (most commonly in the <u>sigmoid colon</u>): a combination of increased intraluminal pressure (e.g., due to chronic <u>constipation</u>) and age-related or physiological <u>weakness</u> of the intestinal wall (See “<u>Diverticulosis</u>.”)

* Inflammation

* Most commonly: <u>chronic inflammation</u> and increased intraluminal pressure → <u>erosion</u> of <u>diverticula</u> wall → inflammation and bacterial translocation

* Rarely: stool becomes lodged in <u>diverticula</u> → obstruction of intestinal lumen → inflammation





![Types of diverticular disease](media/fmp9rifg1vqnheyylfv8qcyj.jpg)

Types of diverticular disease

---

## Clinical features

* Low-grade <u>fever</u>

* <u>Sigmoid colon</u> most commonly affected → <u>left lower quadrant</u> <u>pain</u>

* Possibly tender, palpable mass (pericolonic inflammation)

* Change in bowel habits (<u>constipation</u> in ∼ 50% of cases and <u>diarrhea</u> in 25–35% of cases)

* ↑ Urinary urgency and frequency (in ∼ 15% of cases), <u>sterile pyuria</u>

* <u>Acute abdomen</u>: indicates possible perforation and <u>peritonitis</u>

* Rarely: <u>hematochezia</u>





> [!TIP]
> In elderly or <u>immunocompromised</u> patients, clinical symptoms may only be mild.

---

## Diagnosis

Recommendations in this section are consistent with the 2021 American Gastroenterological Association (<u>AGA</u>) guidelines on the medical <u>management of diverticulitis</u> and the 2018 <u>joint</u> European Association for Endoscopic <u>Surgery</u> (EAES) and Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (<u>SAGES</u>) consensus statements on acute diverticulitis management. [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)




### Approach [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[10]](/library/jR0_5f)[[11]](/library/5gbiDG)




* Suspect acute diverticulitis in adult patients presenting with <u>LLQ</u> <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, and <u>leukocytosis</u>.

* The diagnosis is typically confirmed with imaging, preferably CT abdomen with IV contrast.

* Consider obtaining imaging in patients with:

* An unclear diagnosis

* <u>Immune deficiency</u>

* Poor response to treatment

* Recurrent disease for which <u>surgery</u> is being considered

* Can defer imaging in patients with a prior history of diverticulitis who have: 

* Symptoms similar to previous episodes

* No signs of severe or complicated disease

* Consider <u>colonoscopy</u> to screen for <u>malignancy</u> once the acute phase has resolved and the risk of perforation is reduced.





> [!TIP]
> Women presenting with <u>LLQ</u> <u>pain</u> should receive a <u>pelvic examination</u> in order to assess for gynecologic etiologies. [[11]](/library/5gbiDG)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[10]](/library/jR0_5f)[[12]](/library/c_YaM7)[[13]](/library/0ebexs)




* <u>CBC</u>: <u>leukocytosis</u>, possible <u>anemia</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities, ↑ <u>BUN</u>, ↑ <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>CRP</u>: ↑ <u>CRP</u>

* <u>FOBT</u>: positive in patients with <u>diverticular bleeding</u>

* Consider the following to rule out common differential diagnoses based on <u>pretest probability</u>:

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: to rule out <u>UTI</u> and <u>nephrolithiasis</u>

* Urine or serum <u>β-hCG</u>: to rule out <u>pregnancy</u>, including complications of <u>ectopic pregnancy</u> in all women of reproductive age

* <u>Stool microscopy</u>: to rule out <u>gastroenteritis</u>

* See also “Diagnostics” in “<u>Acute abdomen</u>”.





> [!TIP]
> Diverticulitis is highly likely in patients with <u>LLQ</u> <u>pain</u> and tenderness, no <u>vomiting</u>, and <u>CRP</u> > 50 mg/L. [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)




#### Imaging [[10]](/library/jR0_5f)[[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[14]](/library/CIYqUq)[[15]](/library/Q_YuL7)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)




* CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast [[14]](/library/CIYqUq)

* Indications

* Preferred initial imaging modality for suspected diverticulitis  [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[14]](/library/CIYqUq)

* Diagnostic confirmation in patients with no prior imaging studies [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)

* Staging the severity of diverticulitis (see <u>modified Hinchey classification of diverticulitis</u>)

* Supportive findings

* <u>Colonic</u> outpouching

* Signs of inflammation 

* Bowel wall thickening > 3 mm

* Peridiverticular <u>mesenteric</u> <u>fat stranding</u>

* Complications may also be identified

* Peridiverticular <u>abscess</u>: <u>hypodense</u> collections with peripheral <u>contrast enhancement</u>

* Diverticular perforation: <u>pneumoperitoneum</u>

* <u>Intestinal obstruction</u>: dilated intestinal loops with multiple <u>air-fluid levels</u>

* <u>MRI</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> (without and with IV contrast)

* Indications: suspected diverticulitis in patients with <u>contraindications to CT</u>  [[14]](/library/CIYqUq)

* Findings: similar to those on <u>CT scan</u>

* <u>Ultrasound</u> abdomen

* Indications

* <u>Formal ultrasound</u> is typically considered as an alternative to <u>MRI</u> in patients with <u>contraindications to CT</u>

* <u>Point-of-care ultrasound</u> may be considered as an initial imaging modality and can show findings of <u>complicated diverticulitis</u> (e.g., <u>pneumoperitoneum</u>, free fluid, <u>abscess</u> formation). [[18]](/library/_Sc5XX0)

* Supportive findings: <u>diverticula</u> with surrounding inflammation (<u>hyperechoic</u>), <u>abscess</u> formation (detectable fluid), bowel wall thickening

* <u>Abdominal x-ray</u> [[13]](/library/0ebexs)

* Not useful in diagnosing <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>

* Indications

* Suspected perforation or <u>bowel obstruction</u>

* May be performed as part of the routine workup for <u>acute abdominal pain</u>

* Findings that may be seen in <u>complicated diverticulitis</u> include

* <u>Bowel perforation</u>: <u>pneumoperitoneum</u>

* <u>Bowel obstruction</u>: dilated bowel loops and multiple <u>air-fluid levels</u>

* Screening <u>colonoscopy</u> [[10]](/library/jR0_5f)[[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[19]](/library/pJYLEJ)

* Recommended 6–8 weeks after the resolution of the acute episode to assess the extent of diverticulitis and rule out <u>malignancy</u>  [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[10]](/library/jR0_5f)

* <u>Colonoscopy</u> is contraindicated during an acute episode because of the increased risk of perforation.

* Not required if a recent evaluation of the <u>colon</u> has been performed [[19]](/library/pJYLEJ)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>colonoscopy</u> during the acute phase of diverticulitis because of the risk of perforation!

## Differential diagnoses

* Differential diagnoses of uncomplicated acute diverticulitis

* <u>Crohn disease</u>, <u>ulcerative colitis</u>

* <u>Colorectal cancer</u>

* <u>Intestinal ischemia</u> (<u>ischemic colitis</u>)

* <u>Acute appendicitis</u>

* <u>Ileus</u> , <u>colonic</u> obstruction

* <u>Ectopic pregnancy</u>

* <u>Ovarian torsion</u>

* <u>Ovarian cancer</u>

* <u>Inguinal hernia</u>

* <u>Renal colic</u>

* <u>Urinary tract infection</u>

* Differential diagnoses of perforated diverticulitis: See “<u>Gastrointestinal perforation</u>.”

* See also “<u>Differential diagnoses of acute abdomen</u>.”




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

Recommendations in this section are consistent with the 2021 American Gastroenterological Association (<u>AGA</u>) guidelines on the medical <u>management of diverticulitis</u> and the 2018 <u>joint</u> European Association for Endoscopic <u>Surgery</u> (EAES) and Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (<u>SAGES</u>) consensus statements on acute diverticulitis management. [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)




### Approach [[11]](/library/5gbiDG)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)[[21]](/library/9dbNHs)




* <u>Uncomplicated diverticulitis</u> (Modified Hinchey stage 0 and stage Ia)

* <u>Conservative management</u>   [[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)

* Consider broad-spectrum oral <u>antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u> PLUS <u>metronidazole</u>) in select patient groups.

* <u>Complicated diverticulitis</u> (Modified Hinchey stages Ib–IV)

* Inpatient management with broad-spectrum IV <u>antibiotics</u> is recommended.

* <u>CT-guided percutaneous drainage</u> for <u>abscesses</u> > 4 cm

* Emergency <u>colectomy</u> in patients with generalized <u>peritonitis</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Consider imaging, <u>antibiotic therapy</u>, and surgical consultation early for <u>immunocompromised</u> patients, as they are at high risk of developing severe or complicated disease. [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)




![Management of acute diverticulitis](media/r4evszsd67c1ir73bmdw69yp.jpg)

Management of acute diverticulitis




### <u>Uncomplicated diverticulitis</u> [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[11]](/library/5gbiDG)[[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)




* <u>Antibiotic therapy</u>: Recommended on a selective basis (not routinely) ;  [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[19]](/library/pJYLEJ)[[22]](/library/5UbidG)

* Indications [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[22]](/library/5UbidG)[[23]](/library/T8Y6NI)

* Clinical presentation

* Signs of generalized infection (e.g., <u>fever</u>)

* Persistent symptoms

* <u>Vomiting</u>

* Preexisting conditions

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>

* <u>Frailty</u>

* Comorbidities

* Diagnostic findings

* <u>CRP</u> > 140 mg/L or <u>WBC count</u> > 15,000/mmÂ³

* Fluid collection and/or extensive inflammation on CT

* Options: Consider any of the following broad-spectrum oral <u>antibiotics</u>. [[22]](/library/5UbidG)[[23]](/library/T8Y6NI)

* <u>Metronidazole</u> DOSAGE PLUS one of the following: [[22]](/library/5UbidG)

* <u>Ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE [[22]](/library/5UbidG)

* <u>Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole</u> DOSAGE [[22]](/library/5UbidG)

* <u>Amoxicillin/clavulanate</u> DOSAGE [[22]](/library/5UbidG)

* <u>Moxifloxacin</u> DOSAGE [[22]](/library/5UbidG)

* See also ”<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for intra-abdominal infections</u>.”

* Duration of therapy: 4–7 days [[16]](/library/b_YH57)

* <u>Supportive care</u>

* Relative bowel rest: clear liquid diet until improvement of symptoms

* <u>Analgesics</u> as needed (see “<u>Acute pain management</u>.”) [[11]](/library/5gbiDG)

* First-line treatment for mild to moderate disease: <u>acetaminophen</u> and <u>antispasmodics</u> (e.g., <u>dicyclomine</u>)

* Reserve use of <u>NSAIDs</u> and <u>opioid analgesics</u> for refractory <u>pain</u>.

* <u>Antiemetics</u> as needed

* Disposition and follow-up

* Outpatient treatment [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)

* Follow-up in 2–3 days for evaluation of progression (earlier if symptoms worsen)

* If no improvement: Consider inpatient management; repeat imaging to evaluate for complications.

* Screening <u>colonoscopy</u> (after the first episode) once symptoms have resolved if the patient has not had a <u>colonoscopy</u> within the past year  [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)

* Consider surgical consult for recurrent <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>.

* GI consultation for patients with frequent, recurrent episodes, chronic symptoms, or unclear diagnosis (e.g., possible <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>) [[11]](/library/5gbiDG)[[22]](/library/5UbidG)





> [!TIP]
> Patients without severe symptoms or comorbidities can be managed in an outpatient setting if they have <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>, oral intake is tolerated, and adequate follow-up can be ensured. [[11]](/library/5gbiDG)




### <u>Complicated diverticulitis</u> [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[11]](/library/5gbiDG)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)[[19]](/library/pJYLEJ)[[22]](/library/5UbidG)




* <u>Antibiotic therapy</u>: broad-spectrum IV <u>antibiotics</u> are routinely recommended (see “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for intra-abdominal infections</u>.”)

* Management of complications

* <u>Abscess</u>  [[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)[[24]](/library/h8YcmI)

* Size < 4 cm: trial of <u>conservative management</u> with IV <u>antibiotics</u>

* Signs of improvement in 48–72 hours: Start enteral feeds; consider switching to oral <u>antibiotics</u>.

* No signs of improvement in 48 hours: Repeat imaging and consider percutaneous drainage.

* Size ≥ 4 cm

* <u>Ultrasound</u>- or <u>CT-guided percutaneous drainage</u>

* Consider <u>laparoscopic</u> or open surgical drainage if percutaneous drainage is not feasible.

* Continue IV <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* Send <u>aspirate</u> or <u>pus</u> for cultures and tailor <u>antibiotic</u> treatment accordingly.

* Perforation with generalized <u>peritonitis</u> (i.e., clinical signs of diffuse <u>peritonitis</u> or modified Hinchey stage III and stage IV on imaging): emergency <u>surgery</u> [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)

* Hemodynamically stable patients: <u>laparoscopic</u> or open <u>colectomy</u> and <u>primary anastomosis</u> with/without a temporary diverting <u>stoma</u>

* Critically ill patients: <u>Hartmann procedure</u>

* <u>Bowel obstruction</u>

* See “<u>Treatment of paralytic ileus</u>.”

* See “<u>Management of bowel obstruction</u>.”

* <u>Supportive care</u>

* <u>Complete bowel rest</u> (<u>NPO</u>)

* <u>IV fluids</u> (see <u>IV fluid therapy</u>)

* <u>Analgesics</u> as needed (see <u>acute pain management</u>)

* <u>Antiemetics</u> as needed (see <u>antiemetics</u>)

* Disposition and follow-up: inpatient treatment with <u>surgery</u> and/or interventional radiology consultation

* Screening <u>colonoscopy</u> once symptoms have resolved if the patient has not had a <u>colonoscopy</u> within the past year [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)

* Consider surgical consult for elective <u>colectomy</u> if not performed during admission.





> [!WARNING]
> Obtain an urgent surgical consult in patients with features of generalized <u>peritonitis</u> or <u>sepsis</u>.




### Long-term management




* Elective <u>colectomy</u> ;   [[10]](/library/jR0_5f)[[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)[[19]](/library/pJYLEJ)

* Indications

* Routinely recommended 6–8 weeks after resolution of <u>complicated diverticulitis</u>

* Select groups of patients after resolution of <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>, including:  [[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[17]](/library/S8YyNI)

* Patients at high risk of recurrence with complications  [[13]](/library/0ebexs)

* Patients with persistent abdominal symptoms after resolution of an acute episode

* Chronic complications of diverticulitis (e.g., <u>fistula</u>, <u>colonic strictures</u>)

* Procedure: <u>laparoscopic</u> or open <u>colectomy</u>  [[13]](/library/0ebexs)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)

* <u>Secondary prevention</u> (reducing recurrence risk) [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[16]](/library/b_YH57)[[19]](/library/pJYLEJ)

* Avoid nonaspirin <u>NSAID</u> use, if possible.

* The use of <u>mesalamine</u>, <u>rifaximin</u>, or probiotics to prevent recurrences is no longer recommended. [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)

* See “Prevention” in “<u>Diverticulosis</u>” for <u>primary prevention</u> of diverticulitis, e.g., dietary and lifestyle modification.





![Sigmoid colectomy (in diverticulitis)](media/jt5gopghxzw3l6ujstim1ulo.jpg)

Sigmoid colectomy (in diverticulitis)

## Complications

### Early [[20]](/library/o_Y067)




* Perforation 

* Locally-contained perforation: can lead to the formation of an <u>abscess</u> or <u>phlegmon</u>  [[20]](/library/o_Y067)

* <u>Intraperitoneal</u> perforation

* Caused by:

* Rupture of an inflamed diverticulum;  → free communication with the <u>peritoneum</u> → generalized fecal <u>peritonitis</u>

* Rupture of a diverticular <u>abscess</u> → generalized <u>purulent</u> <u>peritonitis</u>

* Can present with symptoms of <u>acute abdomen</u> and widespread <u>intraperitoneal</u> free air on imaging

* <u>Abscess</u> 

* Peridiverticular localization

* Causes symptoms similar to those of acute diverticulitis

* Suspect an <u>abscess</u> in patients with persistent <u>fever</u> and abdominal <u>pain</u> despite <u>antibiotic</u> treatment.

* <u>Intestinal obstruction</u> (rare) 

* Etiology

* Narrowing due to inflammatory swelling

* Compression through <u>abscesses</u>

* <u>Ileus</u> caused by localized irritation

* Clinical findings

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> and distention

* <u>Constipation</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Acute abdomen</u>

* Bleeding: Although <u>diverticular bleeding</u> occurs commonly as a complication of <u>diverticulosis</u>, it does not frequently coexist with diverticulitis. [[25]](/library/dqXox_)

* <u>Pylephlebitis</u>: Most commonly affecting the <u>superior mesenteric vein</u>, <u>portal vein</u>, and <u>inferior mesenteric vein</u>  [[20]](/library/o_Y067)





### Late [[20]](/library/o_Y067)




* <u>Fistulas</u> ;  [[26]](/library/kR0mMf)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Most commonly colovesical

* Other forms: colovaginal, coloenteric, colocutaneous

* Clinical findings

* <u>Pneumaturia</u> and <u>fecaluria</u>

* May cause recurring <u>urinary tract infections</u>, including <u>urosepsis</u>

* Diagnosis: CT with oral contrast

* Localized thickening of the <u>colon</u> and <u>bladder</u>

* Air or contrast material in the <u>bladder</u>

* Treatment

* Resection and <u>primary anastomosis</u>

* <u>Antibiotics</u> if <u>surgery</u> is not possible

* Recurrent diverticulitis [[5]](/library/0mceV10)

* ∼ 13–23% of patients with <u>uncomplicated diverticulitis</u>  [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)

* Up to 40% of patients with <u>complicated diverticulitis</u>

* Refer patients with recurrence <u>risk factors</u> for specialist consultation to discuss long-term preventative therapy. [[6]](/library/VmcGe10)

* <u>Colon cancer</u>: possibly increased short-term risk following an episode of acute diverticulitis.  [[9]](/library/ohc0UX0)[[27]](/library/cmcae10)
